To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
21 Hz tactile stimuli presented to digits 2 and 3 of the right hand produce a steady-state response in the left hemisphere.

1) the 21 Hz steady‐state response to tactile stimulation is larger on trials when subjects are attending to the stimulus than when they are not; 2) the 21‐Hz response to a digit decreases when that digit is part of a multiple‐digit fusion; and 3) the response to the digit decreases more for fusion than for segregation.

the 21‐Hz steady state response for a finger is larger after than before training to discriminate between 21 Hz stimulation applied to two and three fingers, and that this difference reverses in some subjects over the three day training period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms underlying somatosensory processing in the human brain.
the development of a new approach to the study of human somatosensory processing.
the mechanisms underlying the integration and segregation of tactile information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 21 Hz steady state evoked response to tactile stimulation is a sensitive measure of cortical activation and is sensitive to the effects of training on somatosensory representation.
the fusion of digits 2 +3 + 4, but not 2 + 5, is a reliable phenomenon.
the 21 Hz steady‐state response is sensitive to the strength of activation of the underlying cortical area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 21 Hz steady‐state response can be used as a measure of the strength of cortical activity in somatosensory cortex and that this activity can be altered by experience.
the somatosensory cortex has the capacity to integrate and segregate information, depending on the input.
the 21 Hz steady‐state response for digit 2 + 2 + 1 is larger than for digit 2 or 1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a fixed entity, and it is possible to modify the organization of sensory representations by changing sensory experience.
somatosensyory representations are dynamically altered by the sensory input.

we are able to use the EEG to measure the effects of sensory training on somatosensory cortex, and we are able to measure changes in the somatosensory response to stimulation of a digit that is not directly stimulated by the training.
